documents: Li, R. (2022). Uranium enrichment associated with geothermal alteration: An example from Rehai, Tengchong volcanic area of China. Geological Journal 57(10), 4139-4151 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: the relationship between uranium mineralization and the active geothermal system is rarely examined

steps.action: Poses the question of how uranium is enriched in an active geothermal system, noting that the spring deposits at Tengchong lack elemental geochemistry.
steps.quote: the elemental geochemistry of the spring deposits is critical to understand the mechanism of uranium enrichment associated with geothermal alterations

steps.action: Takes U concentrations of hot spring water and altered sandstones from earlier studies as the starting record.
steps.quote: Previous [...] investigated the geochemical attributes of the hot spring water (U concentrations of 2.6–36 ppb)

steps.action: Samples five geothermal waters (one borehole, three pools, one flow path) in May 2019, filters them, and measures trace metals by ICP-MS and δD and δ18O by laser isotope analyser.
steps.quote: Water samples in this study (collected in May 2019) came from one borehole (ZK37-26), three exposed hot spring pools

steps.action: Checks analytical performance: isotope precision from replicate analyses of three standards, and ICP-MS oxide interference corrections with a tuning solution before calibration.
steps.quote: Analytical precision was better than ±0.6‰ for δD and ± 0.2‰ for δ18O based on replicate analyses of three standards

steps.action: Takes REE concentrations of the Rehai spring waters from published data (Xiao et al. 2010; Hou et al. 2013) and does not measure them.
steps.quote: The rare earth element (REE) concentrations for the hot spring waters from Rehai (see Table S1) were modified from Xiao

steps.action: Collects five spring deposits, then characterizes them by XRD mineralogy, thin sections, SEM-EDS microfabrics and ICP-MS trace elements and REE after acid digestion.
steps.quote: Five hot spring deposits were collected (1 from Dagunguo, 2 from Zhenzhu Spring, 2 from the central Fault surface; Figure 2)

steps.action: Takes trace-element and REE data for the altered Neogene sandstones from Xiao et al. (2017).
steps.quote: The trace element and REE concentrations of altered host rocks (i.e., Neogene sandstones) in Rehai came from Xiao et al. (2017)

steps.action: Compares the water δD-δ18O values with the global and local meteoric water lines (Figure 3).
steps.quote: Almost all the plots of D-O isotopes of hot spring waters distribute along the global meteoric water line (Figure 3).

steps.action: Compares crust-normalized trace-element patterns of waters, deposits and altered sandstones: deposits are enriched relative to water, and sandstones exceed deposits in Pb, Th and U.
steps.quote: Compared to the hot spring water (Figure 4a, Table 1), the hot spring deposits from RHGF are relatively enriched in Zn

steps.action: Concludes from the isotopes and the similarity to Tengchong precipitation that the geothermal water is meteoric.
steps.quote: suggests that meteoric water acts as the main water source of the geothermal waters

steps.action: Proposes enhanced water-rock interaction and/or evaporation, both taken from the literature, for the positive δ18O shift, and assigns both to Zhenzhu Spring without a discriminating test.
steps.quote: may be related to enhanced water-rock interactions (Du et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2016) and/or evaporation due to varying temperatures

steps.action: Infers from shared REE+Y patterns and negative Eu anomalies that the deposits precipitated from spring water under reduced conditions, supported by published negative Eh values.
steps.quote: the distinctly negative Eu anomalies (Figure 5a) indicate their precipitation from hot spring water under reduced conditions

steps.action: Derives from U(VI) mobility and the higher Eh at Zhenzhu that Zhenzhu water should carry more U than Dagunguo water.
steps.quote: the spring water at Zhenzhu Spring is supposed to contain a higher amount of U than that at Dagunguo

steps.action: Checks this expectation against the measured water U concentrations (Table 1) and finds agreement.
steps.quote: This is coherent with the fact that the [...] concentrations of water at Zhenzhu Spring are the highest (Table 1).

steps.action: Compares the HFSE and Cs enrichment and the REE patterns of the altered sandstones with flat terrigenous patterns and with spring water, and infers alteration by hot spring waters with HREE taken up by clays.
steps.quote: indicating that the primary sandstones have been altered by hot spring waters

steps.action: Orders U concentrations across reservoirs: meteoric water ≤ spring water < spring deposits < altered sandstones.
steps.quote: [...] concentrations measured in this study generally follow the order below.

steps.action: Adopts a published mechanism: U leached from granite, carried up faults as uranyl complexes or on silica colloids, and precipitated on decompression.
steps.quote: U in the spring water may come from leaching of U-rich reservoir rocks (e.g., granite) by meteoric water and/or circulated geothermal water.

steps.action: Compares the tamarugite U (27 ppm) with sinters from Nevada and Tibet and with tufas, and compares sandstone U (14-36 ppm) with typical rocks and granite; attributes the sandstone U to adsorption on clays.
steps.quote: The value is much higher than the U concentrations of sinters from northern Nevada

steps.action: Keeps a multi-cycle leaching-transport-decompression-fixation model, citing analogues in Jordan and South Australia, and proposes alteration zones and sulfates as uranium exploration targets.
steps.quote: uranium enrichment is probably a complex process involving multiple cycles of leaching, transportation, decompression, and fixation.

tree.answer: U enrichment in altered sandstones (14-36 ppm) and a tamarugite spring deposit (27 ppm) at Rehai
Concentrations measured directly; the enrichment mechanism is not observed
Explain the U enrichment mechanism in an active geothermal system
Rivals are listed only loosely (water-rock interaction vs evaporation; water-rock vs magma degassing) and not tested
One derived expectation: higher Eh at Zhenzhu implies more U in its water
Conditions found: a single field sampling campaign of natural springs and deposits
Only analytical standards checked; no variation of the inference
Review history not supplied; the paper thanks an anonymous reviewer

end.claim: U enrichment in the Rehai spring deposits and altered sandstones probably results from repeated leaching of U from granites, upward transport along faults by geothermal water, decompression, and fixation in deposits and clay alteration products, so alteration zones are potential uranium exploration targets.

decisive_move.sentence: Ordering U across reservoirs (meteoric water, spring water, spring deposits, altered sandstones) supports the claim of progressive fixation in deposits and alteration zones; without it there is no enrichment claim.

gates.evidence: No mechanism was stated before sampling; the stated aim was only 'To demonstrate the uranium enrichment mechanism' (p. 4139). The one prediction that could have failed (higher Eh at Zhenzhu implies higher water U, p. 4148) was derived after the data were in hand. The main multi-cycle mechanism, taken from Li (1992) and Li et al. (1997), faced no test. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: ICP-MS (Perkin Elmer NexION 350D) for trace elements and REE
IWA 35 EP liquid water isotope analyser for δD and δ18O
Field-emission SEM with energy dispersive spectroscopy (SU 8100)
Water chemistry and REE data from a 16S rRNA microbial census of Tengchong hot springs (Hou et al. 2013)
Typical U concentrations of rocks from Kathren (1984), Radioactivity in the Environment
Adsorption of uranium on clay minerals (Ames et al. 1983; Bao et al. 2021; Davey & Scott 1956)

novelty_claims.quote: For the continental rift-related geothermal system, the hydrothermal alteration zones are rarely studied for uranium exploration.
For the hot spring deposits at Tengchong, however, they are not yet studied in the aspect of elemental geochemistry.
the relationship between uranium mineralization and the active geothermal system is rarely examined

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, so only a final-paper sequence is coded. The paper is single-authored and rests on one sampling campaign (May 2019): five waters and five deposits, with no replicate field samples. Spring-water REE and all altered-sandstone data come from the literature (Xiao et al. 2010, 2017; Hou et al. 2013), yet the U ordering is introduced as 'measured in this study'. The introduction cites prior spring-water U of 2.6-36 ppb, while the paper's own waters give 0-2.7 ppb; the discrepancy is not addressed (inference: possibly a unit or citation error). No uncertainties are given for U in deposits beyond the ~10% ICP-MS accuracy. The proposed U source (leaching of granite) is not tested: no granite or reservoir rocks were sampled and no U isotopes were measured. Rival explanations (water-rock interaction vs evaporation; water-rock interaction vs magma degassing) are listed with 'and/or' and not discriminated. The paper reports no correlation between U and REE+Y but does not use this result. Sub-claims and their statuses: meteoric water source, best_explanation (consistent with published Rehai data); deposits precipitated under reduced conditions, best_explanation; Eh-U expectation at Zhenzhu, matched by data (partly tested, n=2 springs); clay adsorption explaining sandstone U, best_explanation from the literature; alteration zones and sulfates as exploration indicators, none (a recommendation extrapolated beyond the data). Coding the Figure 3 overlay of Hou et al. (2013) data as a replication is the coder's inference: the text does not present it as a check.

disagreements.target: Implied community focus on hot spring deposits (sinters, tufas, travertines) as uranium hosts in geothermal systems
disagreements.support: Altered sandstones at Rehai (14-36 ppm, from Xiao et al. 2017) carry more U than the spring deposits analysed here, so alteration zones are proposed as targets as well.
disagreements.quote: apart from hot spring deposits, the geothermal alteration zones may also be potential exploration targets.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both evaporation and enhanced water-rock interaction (sulfuric acid alteration) at Zhenzhu Spring
alternatives_considered.alternatives: enhanced water-rock interactions; evaporation due to varying temperatures
alternatives_considered.reason: Zhenzhu water is measured at 96 °C with acid fog present, and alteration by sulfuric acid enhances water-rock interaction

alternatives_considered.alternatives: water-rock interactions; magma degassing as the source of dissolved solutes

alternatives_considered.chosen: Differential fractionation among uranyl complexes as the reason the deposit U differs from sinters and tufas
alternatives_considered.alternatives: uranyl carbonate complex; uranyl sulfate complex; uranium adsorbed by SiO2 colloid
